bibliographic.title: Effects of Elevated Temperature and Carbon Dioxide on the Growth and Survival of Larvae and Juveniles of Three Species of Northwest Atlantic Bivalves
bibliographic.title_raw_stored: Effects of Elevated Temperature and Carbon Dioxide on the Growth and Survival of Larvae and Juveniles of Three Species of Northwest Atlantic Bivalves

scope_reason: The paper experimentally examines effects of elevated (marine) temperature and CO2/acidification on bivalve survival and growth.

scope_span.evidence_text: Rising CO 2 concentrations and water temperatures this century are likely to have transformative effects on many coastal marine organisms.

claims.restatement: Raising temperature and CO2 each significantly depressed survival, development, growth and lipid synthesis of M. mercenaria and A. irradians larvae, and the effects were additive.

concept.value: survival, development, growth, and lipid synthesis of M. mercenaria and A. irradians larvae

relation_or_direction.value: increases in temperature and CO 2 each significantly depressed; effects were additive

support_span.evidence_text: Three Species of Northwest Atlantic Bivalves

experimental_condition.value: larvae grown at ~250, ~390, ~750 ppm CO2 and 24 or 28uC (laboratory)

support_span.evidence_text: M. mercenaria and A. irradians larvae were grown at three levels of CO 2 : a high level (,750 ppm CO 2 ), predicted for the year 2100, a modern level (,390 ppm CO 2 ), and a near pre-industrial level (,250 ppm CO 2 ), while at two different temperatures (24 and 28uC).

evidence.evidence_text: Results demonstrated that increases in temperature and CO 2 each significantly depressed survival, development, growth, and lipid synthesis of M. mercenaria and A. irradians larvae and that the effects were additive.

claims.restatement: Higher temperature negatively affected juvenile M. mercenaria and A. irradians but not juvenile C. virginica.

concept.value: juvenile M. mercenaria, A. irradians, C. virginica

relation_or_direction.value: negatively impacted by higher temperatures (M. mercenaria, A. irradians); C. virginica not

support_span.evidence_text: Three Species of Northwest Atlantic Bivalves

experimental_condition.value: juveniles held at 24 or 28uC and ~400 or 1700 ppm CO2 for 45 days (laboratory)

support_span.evidence_text: Ten individuals of each species were placed into triplicate, 10-liter, high-density polyethylene vessels that were maintained in water baths of 24 or 28uC (Table 2).

evidence.evidence_text: Juvenile M. mercenaria and A. irradians were negatively impacted by higher temperatures while C. virginica juveniles were not.

claims.restatement: Larvae were substantially more vulnerable to elevated CO2 than juvenile stages.

concept.value: vulnerability of larval vs juvenile bivalve stages to elevated CO2

relation_or_direction.value: larvae substantially more vulnerable than juveniles

support_span.evidence_text: Three Species of Northwest Atlantic Bivalves

experimental_condition.value: larvae at ~250/390/750 ppm; juveniles at ~400/1700 ppm CO2 (laboratory)

support_span.evidence_text: CO 2 was continuously delivered as described above at ,400 and 1700 ppm

evidence.evidence_text: Larvae were substantially more vulnerable to elevated CO 2 than juvenile stages.

claims.restatement: The authors suggest current and future increases in temperature and CO2 are likely to have negative consequences for coastal bivalve populations.

relation_or_direction.value: increases in temperature and CO2 are likely to have negative consequences (suggested)

experimental_condition.value: inference drawn from the laboratory experiments

evidence.evidence_text: These findings suggest that current and future increases in temperature and CO 2 are likely to have negative consequences for coastal bivalve populations.

rejected_or_ambiguous.evidence_text: Global temperatures are expected to increase 2 to 5uC this century [2].
rejected_or_ambiguous.reason: Cited background projection, not examined by the paper.

rejected_or_ambiguous.evidence_text: Our results demonstrate that interannual variability in temperature and CO 2 are also likely to promote such cycles.
rejected_or_ambiguous.reason: Extrapolation to population boom-bust cycles that the experiments did not test.

rejected_or_ambiguous.evidence_text: Since such high temperatures can be coupled with CO 2 levels exceeding 1,000 ppm [5,24] the negative effects of high temperature and high CO 2 may already be impacting coastal marine bivalve populations [26].
rejected_or_ambiguous.reason: Speculative ('may already'); rests partly on unpublished temperature data cited in the preceding sentence.
